original_value: Most of the existing copy‐move forgery detection (CMFD) methods utilised time‐consuming overlapped block‐based approach. Here, a novel sub‐image approach is proposed for extremely fast and highly accurate detecting of the duplicated forged objects in colour images. The proposed approach consists of few steps. The input coloured images are converted into the hue‐saturation‐value (HSV) colour model. Then, the edges of all objects in the forged image are detected using the Sobel operator. Morphological opening operator and median filter are used in removing unnecessary small objects. The boundaries of the duplicated objects are accurately detected. A bounding rectangle is drawn around the detected object to form a sub‐image. The features of this sub‐image are extracted by using the quaternion polar complex exponential transform moments (QPCETMs) and their invariants to rotation, scaling, and translation. Finally, the duplicated regions are matched via calculating the Euclidian distances and the correlation between the feature vectors. Experiments are performed using different types of duplicated regions. The obtained results of the proposed method are much accurate when compared with the results of the existing methods. Also, the proposed method exhibits high robustness against different attacks such as additive white Gaussian noise, JPEG compression, scaling, and rotation.

result.paraphrase: Most existing copy-move forgery detection (CMFD) methods rely on a time-consuming overlapping block-based approach. In contrast, this work proposes a novel sub-image method for extremely fast and highly accurate detection of duplicated forged objects in color images. The procedure involves several steps: the input color images are first converted to the hue-saturation-value (HSV) color model, after which Sobel operator-based edge detection is applied to all objects in the forged image. Unnecessary small objects are removed using morphological opening and a median filter, and the duplicated objects’ boundaries are then detected precisely. A bounding rectangle is drawn around the detected object to create a sub-image. Features of this sub-image are extracted using quaternion polar complex exponential transform moments (QPCETMs) and their invariance to rotation, scaling, and translation. Finally, duplicated regions are matched by computing Euclidean distances and correlations between the feature vectors. Experiments are carried out on various types of duplicated regions, and the proposed method produces much more accurate results than existing methods. It also shows strong robustness against attacks such as additive white Gaussian noise, JPEG compression, scaling, and rotation.
